title: Grid Cities
objective: After this level you can explain grid street plans from ancient cities to New York.
summary: Grids are ancient (Mohenjo-daro), named for Hippodamus and used by Roman towns and Penn's Philadelphia. New York's 1811 grid was chosen because right-angled houses are cheapest.

cards.headline: In 1811, New York drew a grid over Manhattan, all the way to 155th Street.
cards.body: Look at a map of Manhattan today and you're looking at that decision. The commissioners who drew it later explained why, in one refreshingly blunt sentence. But first: they didn't invent the grid. Not even close.

cards.headline: Older than the Greeks
cards.body: Mohenjo-daro, the largest city of the Indus civilization (about 2600 to 1900 BCE), was laid out with remarkable regularity in about a dozen blocks. Much later, the Greek planner Hippodamus of Miletus, who laid out Athens's port of Piraeus, gave his name to grid plans. He didn't invent them; he just got the credit, like a band covering a song so well that people forget the original.

cards.headline: Easy to measure, easy to divide
cards.body: Many Roman towns were laid out on a grid, with two main streets crossing at right angles. In 1682, William Penn gave Philadelphia a grid, and the idea traveled west with American pioneers for a practical reason: it was the simplest way to divide surveyed land. A grid turns a wild landscape into lots you can number, measure and hand out.

mascot.line: Right angles: loved by surveyors, landowners, and anyone who has ever tried to give directions.

cards.fact: New York chose squares because squares are cheap.
cards.context: The 1811 commissioners wrote that straight-sided, right-angled houses "are the most cheap to build, and the most convenient to live in." No grand theory, no symbolism: a city is mostly homes, and boxy homes are the thriftiest. Manhattan's grid is a cost estimate you can walk around in.

learned: Mohenjo-daro: regular blocks, about 2600 to 1900 BCE
Hippodamus got the name, not the invention

questions.prompt: Why did William Penn's 1682 grid for Philadelphia spread west with American pioneers?

options.label: It copied the street layout of ancient Roman towns
options.rationale: Roman towns used grids too, but that's not why it spread.

options.label: It was the only plan American surveyors were taught
options.rationale: Surveyors knew other plans; the grid was simply the easiest.

options.label: It made every street easier to defend in wartime
options.rationale: Grids weren't chosen for defense here.

options.label: It was the simplest way to divide surveyed land

questions.explanation: Penn's grid traveled west because it was the simplest method of dividing surveyed territory.

questions.prompt: What reason did New York's 1811 commissioners give for their right-angled plan?

options.label: Right-angled houses are cheapest to build
Grids are easier to defend against attack
options.rationale: Their stated reason was cost and convenience.

options.label: It copied Hippodamus's plan of Piraeus
Diagonal streets were forbidden by law
options.rationale: No such rule; they chose rectangles for cost.

questions.explanation: The commissioners said straight-sided, right-angled houses are the most cheap to build and the most convenient to live in.

questions.prompt: Grid Cities: what does Mohenjo-daro's regular layout show about Hippodamus of Miletus?

options.label: He copied it from an Indus trader he met
Grids existed long before his name was attached
He designed Mohenjo-daro himself, as a young man
Grids were invented later, by the Romans
options.rationale: Mohenjo-daro's blocks are far older than Rome.

questions.explanation: Mohenjo-daro (about 2600 to 1900 BCE) was laid out in regular blocks; Hippodamus, in the 5th century BCE, gave his name to grids but didn't invent them.
